title: People judge AI like they judge people
excerpt: AI adoption is not only about capability. People also judge whether the system feels warm, fair, honest, and safe to rely on.
content: One of the strangest things about AI is that we keep insisting it is not human, and then we judge it like a person anyway. This came through strongly in the lesson summary on how people perceive AI. The psychology is very familiar. People judge others on warmth and competence. Are you capable? And also, are your intentions good? Apparently we bring the same mental machinery to AI, which is both understandable and slightly unfair to the machine, since it has no feelings and still somehow gives off “competent but cold intern” energy. The warmth part matters more than people think. Cuddy and colleagues’ warmth-competence model suggests that people often judge intentions before ability. In AI terms, this helps explain why a technically strong system can still be rejected if it feels uncaring, opaque, or misaligned with the user. Mind perception theory adds another layer. People perceive AI through agency and experience. If the AI seems highly agentic, people may think it is more capable. But that also creates a risk: when it fails, the failure may feel less like a malfunction and more like betrayal. A broken calculator is annoying. A confident AI assistant that misleads you after sounding helpful feels personal, even when it is not. This is why adoption is not only a model-quality problem. It is a perception problem. Transparency, reliability, tangibility, immediacy, and even how human-like the system appears can change how people trust it. That does not mean we should make every AI sound like a warm therapist trapped in a browser tab. Please no. It means organisations need to design AI interactions with psychology in mind. My reflection is this: people do not adopt AI because it is powerful in the abstract. They adopt it when it feels useful, understandable, and safe enough to rely on. Competence opens the door. Trust decides whether people walk through.

title: AI leadership still needs someone human in the room
excerpt: AI can help leaders prepare, analyse, and evaluate, but leadership is not only information processing with better formatting.
content: AI leadership sounds impressive until you ask what leadership actually is. If leadership means scheduling, summarising performance notes, comparing options, preparing talking points, or finding patterns in team data, then yes, AI can help a lot. Honestly, some calendar decisions probably deserve to be automated for the emotional health of everyone involved. But leadership is not only information processing. It is influence, trust, timing, courage, and the deeply underrated skill of noticing when everyone in the meeting is pretending to agree because lunch is late. The research summary made this distinction very clear. Employees may be comfortable with AI helping on scheduling, information, budgets, and routine decisions. But they still prefer humans for understanding feelings, building culture, training people, and handling moments where empathy matters. That is not because humans are perfect. Many managers are also powered by caffeine, unread messages, and mild panic. But people still want to believe that the person leading them can understand context. The AI feedback evidence is especially interesting. In one study, AI feedback improved performance when it was simply deployed, but performance dropped once employees were told the feedback came from AI. That says something important: the content of advice is not the whole story. People react to the source. There is also the trust problem. Li and Bitterly find that AI management is perceived as less benevolent than human management. In simpler terms: the AI may be competent, but people are not sure it is on their side. My reflection is this: leaders should absolutely use AI. Use it to prepare better, spot patterns, reduce admin, and become less buried in operational noise. But AI should increase leadership capacity, not replace leadership presence. The leader still has to explain, decide, care, and stand in front of the consequences. Unfortunately, there is no prompt for that part yet.

title: AI is not always the right front desk
excerpt: AI can make service faster, but the research shows people still care deeply about when a human is present, especially when the moment feels personal.
content: AI customer service is one of those ideas that sounds obvious until you become the customer. When everything is simple, I understand the appeal. Reset my password. Track the parcel. Tell me the branch opening hours. Please do not make me wait behind 47 people because I forgot which button means “speak to a human.” In those moments, AI feels like a small mercy. But the research summary reminded me that customers do not resist AI randomly. They resist it when the situation feels emotional, personal, subjective, ethical, or tied to identity. That makes sense. Nobody wants a chatbot to misunderstand their complaint, deny their frustration, and then cheerfully ask, “Was this helpful?” The interesting part is that disclosure is not simple either. Gnewuch and colleagues found that telling customers a human is involved can increase engagement and service quality, but it can also increase employee workload substantially. So “human backup” is not a free trust sticker. It has operational cost. Somewhere, a human still has to read the messy cases, calm the customer, and clean up whatever the AI confidently started. This matters for any business that wants to use AI in high-trust service. The goal should not be to automate the front desk as much as possible. The goal should be to know which moments deserve automation and which moments deserve human presence. AI can handle routine service. It can help less-experienced agents respond faster and better. It can draft, suggest, summarise, and prepare. But when the customer wants care, context, or accountability, the handoff matters. My reflection is this: AI service design should not ask only, “Can the machine answer?” It should ask, “What does the customer need this interaction to feel like?” Sometimes they need speed. Sometimes they need competence. Sometimes they need a person who can say, “I understand why this is upsetting,” and actually mean it.

title: Human-AI teams need instructions, not optimism
excerpt: Human plus AI sounds powerful, but the research keeps reminding me that collaboration does not become useful just because both parties are present.
content: I used to hear “human plus AI” and immediately think, yes, that sounds sensible. Very balanced. Very modern. Very likely to appear on a consulting slide with two overlapping circles and a word like “synergy” in the middle. Then I read more of the research, and the annoying truth is that human-AI collaboration is not automatically better. A meta-analysis by Vaccaro and colleagues looked across more than 100 experiments and found that human-AI combinations often beat humans alone, but do not always beat the stronger standalone partner. In plain English: adding a human to AI, or AI to a human, does not magically create brilliance. Sometimes it creates a meeting. The part I find most useful is that collaboration depends on the task. AI can be very helpful for content creation, drafting, summarising, and routine support. But for decision tasks, especially where the AI is already strong or the human role is unclear, the combination can become messy. The human may over-trust the system, under-trust it, or approve something without really understanding it. So the question is not, “Should we put a human in the loop?” The better question is, “What is the human supposed to do in the loop?” Are they checking facts? Adding context? Catching ethical risks? Improving tone? Making the final decision? Or are they just there so the organisation can say there was oversight? That last version worries me. It gives everyone comfort without giving anyone power. My reflection is this: human-AI teams need instructions, not optimism. The best collaboration is designed around roles, timing, disagreement, and accountability. Otherwise, we are not building a smarter team. We are just creating a workflow where both the human and the machine can be confused at the same time.

title: AI trust travels through people
excerpt: We keep trying to solve AI trust with better models, but trust often travels through people first.
content: I used to think AI trust was mostly about the system. Is it accurate? Is it explainable? Is it secure? Does it hallucinate less than a confident intern with Wi-Fi? All important questions. But the more I read about human-AI collaboration, the more I think trust is much more social than we admit. People do not trust AI in isolation. They watch other people. If a respected colleague uses an AI tool carefully and gets good results, the tool suddenly feels less scary. If a domain expert says, “This is useful here, but dangerous there,” people listen. If a manager quietly ignores the AI, the whole team learns that the official rollout may not matter very much. Trust moves through the room. This makes AI adoption feel less like a software deployment and more like a social network problem. Which is annoying, because social problems are always messier than technical ones. You cannot just patch trust. You cannot install psychological safety version 2.1. You have to build it through behaviour, credibility, and repeated moments where the system proves useful without making people feel stupid. I think this is why so many AI rollouts feel awkward. Companies focus on the tool. They run training. They send the email. They make the deck. The deck always has icons. But they forget the human chain around the tool. Who validates it? Who explains it? Who models careful use? Who says, “No, do not use it for that”? Who gives people permission to question it? My reflection is this: AI trust is not created by AI alone. It is carried by people. Maybe the most important part of an AI system is not only the model, but the humans around it who help others know when to believe it.

title: Human-AI collaboration needs design, not slogans
excerpt: Putting AI into a workflow is easy. Designing the relationship between human judgment and machine output is the hard part.
content: “Human plus AI” sounds so nice. Very balanced. Very future of work. Very suitable for a conference panel where everyone agrees that collaboration is key and then nobody defines collaboration. But the more I read, the more I think human-AI collaboration is not a slogan. It is a design problem. Who does the first draft? Who checks the output? When should the human disagree? When should the AI stay quiet? When does automation free up time, and when does it just create more work disguised as efficiency? These are not small details. These are the whole thing. A bad collaboration design can make both sides worse. The AI gives a confident answer. The human half-checks it. The organisation calls this “human oversight,” even though the human was tired, rushed, and secretly hoping the model was right because the meeting starts in ten minutes. That is not collaboration. That is vibes with a dashboard. Good collaboration is more specific. It knows which tasks should be automated, which tasks need human-AI support, and which tasks should stay human-led because context matters too much. It also allows disagreement. I love that idea. The human is not there to decorate the workflow. The human is there to notice when the system is wrong, incomplete, or optimising for the wrong thing. That means the human role needs to be designed with real power, not ceremonial approval at the end. But that only works if the workflow gives them time, authority, and psychological safety to push back. My reflection is this: AI collaboration is not about putting a machine next to a person and hoping productivity happens. It is about designing the relationship. Otherwise, we are not building human-AI teams. We are just adding another very confident voice to the room.

title: AI makes human judgment harder to hide
excerpt: AI makes the easy parts faster, which means the quality of human judgment becomes much more visible.
content: AI is very good at making people look productive. A report appears. A summary appears. A slide outline appears. A polite email appears, somehow with the phrase “just circling back” even though nobody asked for that energy. At first, this feels like magic. Then it becomes normal. Then the question changes. If everyone can draft faster, summarise faster, and produce decent-looking work faster, what actually separates good work from average work? I think the answer is judgment. Annoying, I know. The hard part remains the hard part. AI can help produce the thing. It cannot always tell you whether the thing matters. It can generate options, but someone still has to choose. It can explain a paper, but someone still has to decide whether the claim is important, whether the evidence is strong, and whether the conclusion survives contact with reality. This is why AI makes human judgment more visible. Before, people could hide behind effort. “I spent all night on this.” Very noble. Very sleep-deprived. Now, effort is less impressive by itself. If AI can help produce a draft in minutes, the value shifts to the thinking behind it. Why this question? Why this argument? Why this decision? What did you reject? What did you notice that the AI missed? That is where expertise shows up. This makes me slightly uncomfortable, because judgment is harder to teach, harder to measure, and harder to fake. But maybe that is a good thing. My reflection is this: AI does not remove the need to think. It removes some of the places where weak thinking used to hide. The future may not belong to people who can produce the most. It may belong to people who know what is worth producing.

title: AI adoption is an emotional experience
excerpt: AI adoption is not only about productivity. It is also about how people feel when a machine enters the relationship.
content: We talk about AI adoption as if people are spreadsheets. Accuracy goes up. Cost goes down. Time saved. Productivity improved. Please proceed to transformation. But people are not spreadsheets. Unfortunately for every implementation plan ever written, people have feelings. They care whether an AI manager feels benevolent. They care whether an empathic response came from a human or a machine. They care whether a chatbot is helping them or trapping them. They care whether AI advice makes them look smart or replaceable. This is why AI adoption is emotional. Not emotional in a soft, fluffy way. Emotional in a very practical way. If employees feel monitored, they resist. If customers feel tricked, they leave. If managers feel less personally responsible because “the system recommended it,” ethics quietly gets slippery. If users feel that AI support is cold, they may reject it even when it is technically competent. The feeling is part of the system. I think companies underestimate this because emotions are harder to put in ROI calculations. “Reduced sense of being cared for” does not fit nicely into a dashboard. But it absolutely affects behaviour. This is especially true in service and leadership. People do not only want speed. They want recognition. They want context. They want someone, or something, to understand why the issue matters. AI can help with that. Sometimes it can even respond more patiently than humans, which is both useful and a little embarrassing for our species. But the emotional meaning changes when people know it is AI. My reflection is this: AI adoption is not just a technical rollout. It is a relationship change. If organisations ignore how AI feels to people, they may get usage without trust, automation without comfort, and efficiency without loyalty. Very efficient failure, basically.

title: People trust AI differently when losses are on the table
excerpt: A story-first look at why people resist AI assistance more when decisions feel like avoiding losses instead of chasing gains.
content: Source: Bockstedt & Buckman (2026) — “Humans’ Use of AI Assistance: The Effect of Loss Aversion on Willingness to Delegate Decisions,” Management Science I used to think algorithm aversion was mostly about trust. People do not trust the machine. The machine feels cold. The machine cannot explain itself properly. Everyone nods, writes “change management” on a slide, and feels productive. This paper makes the story more specific. The issue is not only whether people trust AI. It is also how the decision is framed. When people are rewarded for good performance, they may still prefer human help over AI help. But when the same decision feels like avoiding a loss, the psychology changes. Loss aversion makes people more sensitive to what could go wrong, and that changes whether they are willing to delegate to AI. This is very human. We like to pretend we evaluate tools rationally. In reality, the sentence around the decision matters. “AI can help you gain more” feels different from “AI can help you avoid losing money.” Same tool. Different stomach feeling. That matters for AI adoption at work. If a company introduces AI as a performance booster, employees may hear opportunity. If it introduces AI in a high-stakes loss context, people may hear risk, blame, and “if this goes wrong, who gets yelled at?” Suddenly the resistance looks less irrational. It may be a reasonable response to the emotional framing of the task. My takeaway: adoption is not just a model-quality problem. It is a decision-design problem. If leaders want people to use AI, they need to understand what the decision feels like from the user’s side. Otherwise, even a good tool can arrive wearing the wrong psychological outfit.

title: The future of work is role design under pressure
excerpt: The future of work is not humans versus AI. It is role design under pressure.
content: I am getting tired of the phrase “AI will change work.” Not because it is wrong. Because it is too easy. Of course AI will change work. The more interesting question is how. The papers I have been reading all point in the same direction: the future of work is becoming a role-design problem. Not just “which jobs disappear?” That question is dramatic, but incomplete. The better question is: how do roles change when AI enters the workflow? Middle managers become translators between strategy, employees, customers, and AI systems. Leaders become AI-supported sense-makers, but still have to do the human part. Workers need to know when to trust the machine and when to push back. Domain experts become interpreters of AI outputs. Customers may interact with hybrid agents where the boundary between human and machine is not always obvious. Everything becomes a little more blended. And blended work needs design. Otherwise, people end up with strange half-roles. The human is responsible but not empowered. The AI recommends but does not explain enough. The manager is accountable for a system they do not fully understand. The customer is told help is available, but nobody is sure whether help means bot, human, or emotional obstacle course. This is where organisations need to grow up quickly. AI is not just a tool added to existing jobs. It changes the shape of the job. What should humans still own? What should AI handle? What needs escalation? What needs judgment? What needs care? My reflection is this: the future of work is not humans versus AI. It is role design under pressure. Companies that get this right will not simply automate tasks. They will redesign responsibility, learning, trust, and decision-making around the new reality. Much harder than buying software. Much more important too.

title: The ABCs of who actually benefits from working with AI
excerpt: A story-first look at why AI does not help everyone equally, and why the people who benefit most may not be the ones we expect.
content: Source: Caplin et al. (2025) — “The ABCs of Who Benefits from Working with AI,” Management Science The most tempting sentence in AI is: “AI makes people more productive.” It sounds clean. It sounds measurable. It sounds like something that belongs in a board deck with a blue gradient. But the more interesting question is: which people? This paper looks at who actually benefits from working with AI. I like that framing because it refuses to treat “workers” as one big identical blob. People come into AI collaboration with different skills, confidence levels, habits, and weaknesses. Naturally, AI does not land on everyone the same way. That feels obvious once you say it, but organisations often skip this step. They roll out one tool, one training session, one cheerful email from leadership, and then act surprised when usage patterns are messy. Some people become dramatically faster. Some barely change. Some trust the output too much. Some refuse to touch it because they had one bad answer and now the entire technology is personally offensive. The useful lesson is that AI benefits are distributed. A tool can help lower-performing workers by giving them structure. It can help high-performing workers by speeding up routine work. It can also create very different outcomes depending on whether the person knows how to ask, check, revise, and decide. So the question is not simply whether AI works. The question is who it works for, under what conditions, and what support they need to use it well. My takeaway: AI transformation should not be designed for an imaginary average employee. That person does not exist. The real work is understanding the different groups of users, then building training and workflows around them. Less glamorous than a launch announcement, but much more useful.

title: Will governance help AI adoption, or quietly stop it?
excerpt: I want to understand whether AI governance gives people confidence to move, or gives them one more reason to do nothing.
content: I keep coming back to one question: will a clear AI governance framework help people adopt AI, or will it make them more afraid to even try? This is one of the reasons I chose this research topic. Not because I enjoy governance documents. Nobody wakes up excited to read a 47-page policy unless something has gone slightly wrong in their life. But I do want to understand what actually drives AI adoption inside organisations. Do companies adopt AI because they genuinely want to become better? Because they want to look innovative? Because competitors are doing it? Because someone senior went to a conference, heard the word “agentic”, and came back with dangerous enthusiasm? Probably all of the above. But I am also interested in the opposite question: when people do not adopt AI, why not? Is it because they do not understand it, or because they understand just enough to be scared? Scared of making the wrong decision. Scared of losing their job. Scared of damaging their reputation. Scared that if the AI makes a mistake, everyone will ask why they approved it in the first place. And honestly, that fear makes sense. AI adoption is rarely just a technology issue. It is a people issue, a trust issue, and sometimes an office politics issue wearing a very serious suit. So maybe good governance is not supposed to slow people down. Maybe it is supposed to give people enough confidence to move. The real question is whether governance feels like a map or a warning sign. Because if people experience AI governance as protection, adoption may grow. But if they experience it as punishment waiting to happen, they may do the safest thing of all: nothing.

title: Trusting an AI teammate depends on who else trusts it
excerpt: A story-first look at why trust in AI teammates is not formed alone. People watch how other humans treat the AI too.
content: Source: Erengin et al. (2024) — “You, Me, and the AI: The Role of Third-Party Human Teammates for Trust Formation Toward AI Teammates,” Journal of Organizational Behavior Trust in AI sounds like a one-on-one relationship. Me and the tool. Me and the chatbot. Me and the system that keeps confidently suggesting things at suspicious speed. But in real teams, trust is social. This paper studies how third-party human teammates shape trust toward an AI teammate. In plain English: if I see someone else on my team treating the AI as useful, competent, and trustworthy, that changes how I see it too. This feels very real. Most people do not form opinions about workplace technology in isolation. They watch what the credible people around them do. If the respected teammate uses the AI carefully and gets good results, the system feels safer. If that teammate rolls their eyes every time the AI appears, the AI is already losing before it speaks. This matters because companies often treat AI adoption like an individual training issue. Teach the user. Give the user a guide. Send the user a webinar link that they will absolutely not watch. But if AI is entering team workflows, the social layer matters. People learn not only from documentation, but from other people’s behaviour. Trust travels through the team. That is both good and dangerous. Good, because trusted colleagues can help normalise careful use. Dangerous, because one influential sceptic can quietly poison adoption, sometimes for valid reasons, sometimes because the first demo was terrible and nobody recovered emotionally. My takeaway: AI teammates need social onboarding, not just technical onboarding. Leaders should pay attention to who models the behaviour, who validates the tool, and who helps others interpret it. Trust is not installed. It spreads.

title: From AGI to ASI, the scary question is what happens after the finish line
excerpt: A story-first look at why reaching AGI is not the end of the AI story. It may be the start of a much harder one.
content: Source: Genewein et al. (2026) — “From AGI to ASI,” Google DeepMind AGI is often treated like the finish line. As if the whole AI race is a marathon, and one day someone breaks the tape, everyone claps, and the field politely becomes stable. This report asks the more uncomfortable question: what happens after AGI? That is where the conversation moves from artificial general intelligence to artificial superintelligence. And honestly, this is the part where the room should probably get quieter. The report frames machine intelligence as a continuum. Human-level general intelligence is not necessarily the endpoint. It could be a milestone on the way to systems that continue improving, discovering, planning, and operating at levels far beyond human capability. This matters because many current debates are still stuck on whether AGI is possible, close, overhyped, or already secretly here depending on how dramatic someone’s LinkedIn post is. But strategy needs to ask the next question too. If AGI arrives, what institutions govern the transition after it? Who decides how far systems are allowed to self-improve? What safety mechanisms still work when the system becomes better than humans at finding loopholes? What does control mean when the thing being controlled is more capable than the controller? These are not small questions. They are also not questions we should save for the day after AGI arrives. That would be like designing airport safety after the plane has already taken off. My takeaway: AGI is not the end of the story. It is the point where the governance problem becomes sharper. The real challenge is not only building powerful intelligence. It is surviving the transition from impressive systems to systems that may no longer fit inside human assumptions.

title: Customers react differently when they know a human is behind the AI
excerpt: A story-first look at hybrid service agents and why disclosing human involvement can change how customers treat AI-powered support.
content: Source: Gnewuch et al. (2024) — “More Than a Bot: The Impact of Disclosing Human Involvement on Customer Interactions with Hybrid Service Agents,” Information Systems Research Customer service AI has a strange identity problem. Is it a bot? Is it a human? Is it a bot secretly helped by a human? Is it a human trapped behind software that says “I understand your frustration” with suspicious calm? This paper looks at hybrid service agents, where AI and humans are both involved in customer interactions. The key question is what happens when customers are told that a human is involved behind the system. That disclosure sounds small, but it changes the social situation. When customers think they are dealing only with a bot, expectations shift. They may become more impatient, more forgiving, or more suspicious depending on the context. But when they know a human is involved, the interaction can feel more accountable. There is someone behind the curtain. Someone, theoretically, who can understand nuance and perhaps rescue the conversation before it becomes a copy-paste tragedy. This matters because companies often focus on whether automation works operationally. Can it answer faster? Can it reduce ticket volume? Can it stop customers from typing “agent” thirteen times like a spell? But service is not just information transfer. It is emotional management. Customers want answers, yes, but they also want to feel that their problem has landed somewhere human enough to care. That is why disclosure is not just a legal or design detail. It is part of trust design. My takeaway: hybrid service agents need honesty about what is happening. If humans are involved, say so clearly. If AI is involved, say that too. Customers do not necessarily hate automation. They hate feeling tricked, ignored, or trapped in a service maze wearing a chatbot costume.

title: Whether people follow algorithmic advice depends on incentives and framing
excerpt: A story-first look at why people do not respond to algorithmic advice in a vacuum. Incentives and framing shape whether advice is used.
content: Source: Greiner et al. (2026) — “Incentives, Framing, and Reliance on Algorithmic Advice: An Experimental Study,” Management Science Algorithmic advice sounds like a simple thing. The model gives a recommendation. The human looks at it. The human decides whether to follow it. Very tidy. Very unrealistic. In real life, people do not evaluate advice in a vacuum. They evaluate it inside a messy little room filled with incentives, accountability, fear, habits, and the possibility of looking foolish. This paper studies how incentives and framing affect reliance on algorithmic advice. That is important because so many organisations assume adoption is mostly about accuracy. Make the model better, and people will follow it. Maybe. But not always. If the reward structure punishes visible mistakes more than quiet missed opportunities, people may avoid algorithmic advice even when it is useful. If the advice is framed as replacing judgment, people may resist. If it is framed as supporting judgment, the same recommendation may feel less threatening. This is why two teams can receive the same AI tool and behave completely differently. One sees helpful support. The other sees future blame arriving early in a very polished interface. This is very human. People are not just asking, “Is the algorithm right?” They are asking, “If I follow this and it fails, who owns the failure?” They are asking, “Will I look lazy?” They are asking, “Does using this make me smarter, or does it make me replaceable?” Those questions do not appear in the model output, but they shape behaviour. My takeaway: algorithmic advice needs incentive design, not just interface design. If leaders want people to use AI well, they need to align the social and organisational context around it. Otherwise the advice may be accurate, available, and politely ignored.

title: Bot gender matters most when the service moment is tense
excerpt: A story-first look at why bot gender can shape customer reactions in high-tension service contexts.
content: Source: Guo et al. (2025) — “Does Bot Gender Matter? Theory and Evidence From a High-Tension Service Context,” MIS Quarterly I have complicated feelings about gendered bots. On one hand, people respond to social cues. Voice, name, tone, avatar, even tiny design choices can change how a customer interprets a service interaction. On the other hand, the idea of giving a chatbot a gender so customers behave differently feels like we have taken human stereotypes, put them in a software box, and called it strategy. Very efficient. Very uncomfortable. This paper studies whether bot gender matters in a high-tension service context. That context is important. When customers are calm, bot design may feel like decoration. But when they are angry, anxious, or waiting for help, every social cue becomes louder. The customer is not just processing information. They are managing emotion. If a bot is perceived through gendered expectations, that can change trust, patience, blame, or willingness to continue the interaction. It may affect whether the customer experiences the bot as helpful, competent, warm, irritating, or somehow all four in the same chat window. The practical point is not that companies should rush to gender every bot. Please no. The point is that social design choices are never neutral. A name, voice, or persona can activate assumptions that designers may not intend but customers still bring into the interaction. That matters especially in service settings where the customer already feels wronged. My takeaway: bot gender is not a cute branding detail. It is a social cue with consequences. If companies use it, they need to understand what assumptions it triggers, who benefits, and whether the design is solving a service problem or simply borrowing stereotypes to make automation feel softer.

title: AI trust is built through networks, not one-on-one magic
excerpt: A story-first look at how domain experts help build trust in AI-based counterparts through triadic relationships.
content: Source: Hanelt et al. (2026) — “Opening the Network of Trust: How Domain Experts in Triadic Relationships Build Trust in AI-Based Counterparts,” MIS Quarterly We often talk about trusting AI as if it happens directly. A person meets a system. The system performs. Trust either appears or collapses dramatically, like a bad first date. This paper suggests the trust story is more networked than that. Domain experts can help other people build trust in AI-based counterparts. In other words, trust does not only come from the AI’s behaviour. It also comes through relationships with humans who understand the domain and can interpret what the AI is doing. That makes sense. Most users are not in a position to evaluate AI deeply. They can see outputs, but they may not know whether those outputs are meaningful, risky, or just confidently formatted nonsense. A domain expert becomes a translator. They help explain when the AI is useful, where its limits are, and what kind of judgment still belongs to humans. This is especially important in professional settings. If a doctor, analyst, engineer, or manager says, “This system is useful here, but be careful there,” that carries more weight than a vendor brochure saying “trusted AI solution” in a font that looks expensive. Trust becomes triadic: user, AI, expert. That is a much more realistic model of adoption. It also means organisations should stop assuming trust can be created by training videos alone. People trust through people. Especially when the technology is complex. My takeaway: AI trust is social infrastructure. Domain experts are not just users of AI. They are trust-builders, interpreters, and boundary setters. If companies ignore that role, they may deploy technically strong systems into environments where nobody knows how to believe them properly.

title: Managing human-AI teams can quietly bend leaders' ethics
excerpt: A story-first look at the dark side of managing human-AI collaboration, where leaders may become more morally flexible than they realise.
content: Source: He et al. (2026) — “The Dark Side of Managing Human-AI Collaborations: Implications for Leaders’ Moral Relativism and Unethical Behaviour,” Journal of Management Studies Most human-AI collaboration papers are optimistic. Humans bring judgment. AI brings speed. Everyone collaborates beautifully. Productivity rises. Somewhere, a consultant creates a framework with three circles. This paper is interested in the darker side. It asks what managing human-AI collaboration does to leaders themselves. The argument is uncomfortable: when leaders manage work split between humans and AI, they may become more morally relativistic, which can increase unethical behaviour. That sounds dramatic, but I can see the logic. AI creates distance. Decisions feel more technical. Responsibility becomes easier to blur. If a recommendation came from a system, a dashboard, or a model, leaders may start treating moral choices as more flexible. Not evil, necessarily. Just slightly easier to rationalise. That is how many ethical problems begin. The scary part is that this can look like professionalism from the outside. The leader is not emotional. The process is data-driven. The decision has documentation. Lovely. Except the moral weight may have quietly slipped out of view. Not with someone announcing, “Today I will behave badly.” More often, it starts with ambiguity. The system suggested it. The metric required it. The process allowed it. The human becomes the manager of a machine-mediated decision and quietly feels less personally responsible. Very convenient. Very dangerous. The paper also points to individual differences, such as leaders’ need for cognitive closure. Some leaders may be more vulnerable when AI makes messy decisions feel neatly packaged. My takeaway: AI governance is not only about controlling the system. It is also about watching what the system does to human decision-makers. Leaders need ethical guardrails, not just AI dashboards. Otherwise, collaboration with AI may not remove human weakness. It may simply give it better cover.

title: AI can boost employee creativity, but only under the right conditions
excerpt: A story-first look at when and how AI augments employee creativity at work.
content: Source: Jia et al. (2024) — “When and How Artificial Intelligence Augments Employee Creativity,” Academy of Management Journal Creativity has a strange relationship with AI. Some people think AI will make everyone more creative. Some think it will flatten everything into the same smooth beige paste. Both arguments have receipts. This paper looks at when and how AI augments employee creativity, which is exactly the more useful question. Because AI does not automatically make people creative. It gives suggestions. It expands possibilities. It offers combinations that may be surprising, useful, or mildly cursed. Whether that becomes creativity depends on the human using it. In workplace terms, AI can act like a cognitive resource. It can help employees generate more ideas, escape obvious patterns, and see alternatives they might not have reached alone. That is the good version. But creativity is not just more ideas. Anyone who has opened an AI-generated list of 50 suggestions knows this. Quantity arrives very quickly. Quality arrives wearing noise-cancelling headphones and asking for patience. The human still needs taste, context, and the ability to choose. Without that, AI can create the illusion of creativity while producing ideas that are technically varied but strategically useless. This is where conditions matter. Employees need the motivation, skill, and support to work with AI actively, not just accept its first answer like it came down from a mountain. The best use of AI for creativity may be less like outsourcing imagination and more like having a slightly chaotic brainstorming partner who never gets tired. Useful, yes. Final decision-maker, no. My takeaway: AI can augment creativity when humans stay engaged as editors, judges, and sense-makers. The danger is not that AI gives us ideas. The danger is that we stop asking whether those ideas are any good.

title: Middle managers are becoming translators for AI service teams
excerpt: A story-first look at how AI changes the work characteristics of middle managers leading AI service teams.
content: Source: Koponen et al. (2025) — “Work Characteristics for Middle Managers Leading AI Service Teams,” Journal of Service Research Middle managers already had a difficult job. They sit between strategy and reality, which is basically a polite way of saying they receive pressure from above and confusion from below. Now add AI service teams. This paper studies how middle managers experience AI integration in service work, especially in financial services. The useful point is that AI does not enter the organisation as one simple thing. Sometimes it feels like a technical tool. Sometimes it feels like a coworker. Sometimes it feels like a mysterious new team member that never sleeps and occasionally needs supervision. That changes the manager’s work. Managers are no longer only coordinating people. They are coordinating relationships between people and systems. They have to understand what the AI can do, what it should not do, when employees trust it too much, when they ignore it too much, and how customers experience the result. This is a lot. It also means middle managers become translators. They translate strategy into workflows. They translate AI outputs into operational decisions. They translate employee concerns upward. They translate customer pain into system improvements. If that sounds exhausting, it is because it probably is. The interesting part is that AI does not remove management work. It changes the texture of it. Less pure supervision. More sense-making. Less “did the employee do the task?” More “how do human and AI roles fit together without making everyone quietly resent the dashboard?” My takeaway: AI transformation depends heavily on middle managers, even though they are rarely the stars of the AI story. If companies want AI service teams to work, they need to support the people managing the messy middle. That is where adoption becomes real.

title: People distrust AI managers because they do not feel benevolent
excerpt: A story-first look at why employees may trust AI management less than human management, even when the AI seems competent.
content: Source: Li & Bitterly (2024) — “How Perceived Lack of Benevolence Harms Trust of Artificial Intelligence Management,” Journal of Applied Psychology An AI manager can be efficient. It can schedule. Track. Allocate. Evaluate. Remind. Measure. Optimise. Basically everything a workplace loves to turn into a dashboard. But this paper points to a problem that dashboards rarely solve: benevolence. Across field and experimental evidence, the authors find that AI management is perceived as less benevolent than human management. That matters because trust in a manager is not only about ability. It is also about whether the person, or system, is believed to care about your interests. This is where AI management gets awkward. A human manager may be imperfect, biased, tired, distracted, or replying to messages at a worrying hour. But employees can still imagine that the manager understands their situation. Maybe they care. Maybe they can make an exception. Maybe they can see context. AI management feels different. Even if it is accurate, it can feel indifferent. It may apply rules consistently, but consistency is not the same as care. If the system denies a request, changes a schedule, or evaluates performance, the employee may experience it as cold rather than fair. That is a serious adoption problem. Especially in management, because people accept difficult decisions more easily when they believe the decision-maker has at least considered their welfare. AI may be consistent, but consistency without care can feel like bureaucracy with better software. Because people do not only ask, “Is this manager capable?” They ask, “Is this manager on my side at all?” If the answer feels like no, trust suffers. My takeaway: AI management cannot rely on competence alone. Organisations need to design for perceived care, appeal, context, and human backup. Otherwise AI may become the manager that never forgets a metric but never understands a person. Efficient, yes. Trusted, not necessarily.

title: AI-augmented leadership works when leaders still do the human part
excerpt: A story-first look at how leaders can work with AI to improve team performance without outsourcing leadership itself.
content: Source: Liu et al. (2026) — “AI-Augmented Leadership: How, Why, and When Leaders’ Collaboration With AI Enhances Team Performance,” Journal of Organizational Behavior AI-augmented leadership sounds powerful. Also slightly suspicious. Because leadership is one of those words people use when they mean everything from setting direction to sending calendar invites with confidence. This paper looks at how leaders’ collaboration with AI can enhance team performance. The important word is collaboration. Not replacement. Not “let the AI lead because it has better bullet points.” Collaboration. AI can help leaders process information, see patterns, prepare communication, support decisions, and respond faster. That can improve team performance when the leader uses AI to become more attentive and effective. But leadership is not only information processing. Teams need meaning. They need trust. They need someone to notice when the official plan and reality are no longer speaking. They need judgment about timing, emotions, conflict, and whether everyone is pretending to understand the strategy because the meeting is almost over. AI can support those things, but it cannot fully own them. That is the line I think leaders need to keep clear. If AI helps a leader ask better questions, prepare better, or see risks earlier, wonderful. If AI becomes a shield that lets the leader avoid difficult human conversations, less wonderful. Very modern, but less wonderful. The value of AI-augmented leadership depends on whether the leader stays engaged. AI should increase leadership capacity, not reduce leadership presence. My takeaway: leaders can absolutely use AI to become better leaders. But the human part does not disappear. If anything, it becomes more visible. The AI can help with analysis and preparation. The leader still has to create trust, make calls, and stand in front of the consequences.

title: Rideshare drivers show algorithm aversion is not irrational stubbornness
excerpt: A story-first look at algorithm aversion among ridesharing drivers and why ignoring the algorithm can sometimes make sense.
content: Source: Liu et al. (2026) — “Algorithm Aversion: Evidence from Ridesharing Drivers,” Management Science Algorithm aversion is often described like a human flaw. The model knows better. The human ignores it. Silly human. Please attend another training session. But ridesharing makes the story more interesting. Drivers live inside algorithmic management. The platform suggests, nudges, prices, routes, matches, rewards, and sometimes changes the rules in ways that feel like they were designed by a committee of spreadsheets. So when drivers resist algorithmic recommendations, is that irrational? Maybe not. A driver has local context the platform may not fully capture. They know traffic quirks, customer patterns, neighbourhood risk, waiting spots, event timing, and the emotional cost of being sent somewhere inconvenient for a theoretically optimal trip. The algorithm sees a lot. The driver sees differently. That difference matters. In platform work, algorithm aversion may reflect distrust, yes, but it can also reflect experience. Workers learn when the system is useful and when it is optimising for the platform more than for them. If the recommendation feels misaligned with their own goals, resistance becomes a form of self-protection. This is why algorithmic management is so tricky. The platform may think it is providing guidance. The worker may experience it as control. Same recommendation, different politics. And when people feel controlled by a system they cannot question, they do not simply become obedient. They adapt, evade, second-guess, or build their own informal rules. My takeaway: algorithm aversion is not always a trust deficit. Sometimes it is a signal that the worker sees incentives the model ignores. If platforms want better cooperation, they need more transparency, alignment, and respect for local human knowledge. Otherwise the algorithm becomes just another boss people learn to manage.

title: One plus one can be bigger than two when humans and machines share information
excerpt: A story-first look at why human-machine collaboration depends on information flow, not just model accuracy.
content: Source: Lu & Zhang (2025) — “1 + 1 Bigger Than 2: Information, Humans, and Machines,” Information Systems Research Human plus machine sounds like it should automatically be better. After all, the human has judgment. The machine has scale. Put them together and surely we get something beautiful, like productivity with better lighting. Except collaboration is not magic. This paper focuses on information, humans, and machines. The title suggests the key idea nicely: one plus one can be bigger than two, but only when the information relationship works. That is the part many AI implementations underestimate. It is not enough to put a model beside a human and call it collaboration. The human needs to know what the model knows, what it does not know, and when its recommendation should matter. The machine may need human input to improve or contextualise decisions. If information flows badly, the team can become worse than either side alone. Very relatable. Anyone who has worked in a team knows that adding more smart people does not guarantee a better outcome. Sometimes it just creates a longer meeting. Human-machine collaboration has the same problem. The value comes from complementarity. The human and machine need different useful information, and the workflow needs to let that information meet at the right moment. If the machine only produces an answer without context, the human may overtrust or undertrust it. If the human ignores the machine’s signal, the model becomes decoration. Expensive decoration. My takeaway: the future of human-AI collaboration is not simply about better algorithms. It is about better information design. What does each side know? What should each side reveal? When should the handoff happen? That is where one plus one might finally become bigger than two.

title: AI empathy can be good, but people still care who they think is listening
excerpt: A story-first look at why people value empathy differently when they believe it comes from a human versus AI.
content: Source: Rubin et al. (2025) — “Comparing the Value of Perceived Human versus AI-Generated Empathy,” Nature Human Behaviour AI can now write very comforting sentences. Sometimes too comforting. The kind of sentence that makes you think, “This is emotionally intelligent,” followed immediately by, “Wait, does it actually care, or is it just very good at sounding like it cares?” This paper studies perceived human versus AI-generated empathy. Across studies, empathic responses were labelled as coming from either humans or AI, and people evaluated them differently. The core tension is fascinating. AI can produce responses that look empathic. It can acknowledge feelings, reflect pain, offer support, and avoid saying the terrible things humans sometimes say when trying to help. Honestly, some humans could use the training data. But people still care about attribution. A response believed to come from a human can feel more valuable because empathy is not only about the words. It is also about the belief that another conscious person noticed you, cared, and chose to respond. That is hard for AI to fully replicate. This matters for emotional support, healthcare, customer service, coaching, and any context where organisations are tempted to scale empathy. Scaling empathy sounds wonderful until you realise empathy may lose something when people know it is automated. The practical question is not whether AI can write supportive text. It can. The question is what kind of support people think they are receiving, and whether disclosure changes the meaning of the interaction. My takeaway: AI empathy may be useful, but it is not the same social object as human empathy. The words matter, but so does the imagined listener behind them. Sometimes people do not just need a good response. They need to believe someone is there.

title: Generative AI boosts creativity most for people who know how to think about thinking
excerpt: A story-first look at why generative AI affects creativity differently depending on employees' metacognitive strategies.
content: Source: Sun et al. (2025) — “How and for Whom Using Generative AI Affects Creativity: A Field Experiment,” Journal of Applied Psychology AI creativity tools are easy to oversell. Give everyone generative AI, and suddenly the workplace becomes more creative. Ideas everywhere. Innovation blooming. Someone from strategy says “step change” and everyone pretends not to flinch. This paper asks a better question: how and for whom does generative AI affect creativity? The “for whom” part matters. The authors focus on metacognitive strategies, which is a fancy way of saying people who monitor and regulate their own thinking. They do not just produce ideas. They think about how they are producing ideas. That skill changes how AI is used. If someone has strong metacognitive habits, AI becomes a resource. They can use it to expand options, test directions, challenge assumptions, and then choose. They stay in charge of the thinking process. If someone lacks those habits, AI can become a shortcut that feels productive but may not lead to better creativity. The person receives outputs, but does not necessarily know how to interrogate them. This is exactly why AI training should not only teach prompting. Prompting is useful, yes. But the deeper skill is reflective thinking. What am I trying to solve? Why is this suggestion good or bad? What assumption is hiding here? What would make this idea actually useful? Without that, AI can produce a lot of options and still leave you with no taste. Which is basically a buffet problem, but for ideas. My takeaway: generative AI can support creativity, but it rewards people who know how to manage their own thinking. The future creative advantage may not be having AI. Everyone has AI. It may be knowing how to think with it without letting it drive.

title: AI helps experienced workers differently from senior workers
excerpt: A story-first look at why task experience and seniority do not produce the same benefits when workers team with AI.
content: Source: Wang et al. (2024) — “Friend or Foe? Teaming Between Artificial Intelligence and Workers with Variation in Experience,” Management Science Experience is one of those words that sounds simple until you actually measure it. Someone can have experience doing a specific task many times. Someone else can have seniority, broad organisational knowledge, and the confidence of a person who has survived many meetings. Those are not the same thing. This paper studies how workers with different types of experience team with AI, using a field study in medical chart coding. The finding is useful because it separates narrow task experience from broader seniority. AI helped workers with greater task-based experience. That makes sense. If you know the work deeply, AI can become a fast assistant. You can spot when it is helpful, catch mistakes, and use it to move faster. But senior workers did not necessarily gain as much. The lower productivity lift was linked to lower trust in AI, not seniority itself. I find this very believable. People with broad experience may have stronger habits, stronger judgment, and more reasons to question a system. Sometimes that scepticism protects quality. Sometimes it blocks useful support. The line is not always obvious. This complicates the lazy idea that AI helps juniors and threatens seniors. Reality is messier. AI may help people most when they have enough task knowledge to use it well and enough openness to actually use it. Too little knowledge, and they may not know what to check. Too little trust, and the tool sits there like an expensive ornament. My takeaway: AI training should not treat experience as one thing. Task experts, senior employees, and newcomers may need different support. The goal is not blind trust. It is calibrated trust, which is much less catchy but much more useful.

title: Perfume creation shows why human-AI collaboration needs translation
excerpt: A story-first look at cognitive asymmetry in human-AI collaboration through the surprisingly useful world of perfume creation.
content: Source: Yokoi et al. (2026) — “Organizing Across Cognitive Asymmetry in Human-AI Collaboration: A Study of Perfume Creation,” Strategic Management Journal Perfume creation is such a perfect place to study human-AI collaboration. Because perfume is not just a formula. It is memory, taste, culture, body, mood, and someone saying “this smells like late afternoon in a hotel lobby” as if that is a normal operational requirement. This paper studies human-AI collaboration in perfume creation and introduces the idea of cognitive asymmetry. Humans have tacit, embodied knowledge. AI has codified knowledge. Both can be powerful, but they do not naturally speak the same language. That creates a representational gap. I love that phrase because it explains so many AI projects. The human knows something but cannot fully express it. The AI produces something but does not fully understand the world behind the request. Between them sits a gap full of prompts, revisions, misunderstandings, and occasionally something interesting. The study identifies representational integration as the organising process that bridges the gap. Humans and GenAI coordinate by allocating tasks based on their cognitive advantages, converting knowledge between tacit and codified forms, and steering outputs as the problem evolves. In simpler terms: humans translate taste into instructions, AI turns codified knowledge into options, and humans keep steering because the work changes as it unfolds. That feels like the real future of creative AI. Not AI replacing human taste. Not humans ignoring AI. More like a strange collaboration where the human keeps translating the unsayable into something the machine can work with. My takeaway: human-AI collaboration needs translation work. The value is not only in the output. It is in learning how to move between human intuition and machine representation without losing the thing that made the work meaningful in the first place.

title: AI chat can engage customers, but the handoff still matters
excerpt: A story-first look at AI in online customer chats and why engagement depends on more than fast automated replies.
content: Source: Zhang & Narayandas (2026) — “Engaging Customers with AI in Online Chats: Evidence from a Randomized Field Experiment,” Management Science Online chat is where customer patience goes to be tested. You open the little bubble. The bot says hello. You explain your problem. The bot asks you to explain it again in a slightly different way. Somewhere around message four, your soul leaves your body. So I am always interested in studies that test AI chat in the real world, not just in a demo where everyone behaves nicely. This paper looks at engaging customers with AI in online chats through a randomized field experiment. The practical question is simple: can AI improve customer engagement in service conversations? It probably can, but the hard part is not just response speed. AI can answer quickly, scale support, and handle common questions. That is useful. But customer engagement depends on whether the interaction feels relevant, capable, and worth continuing. A fast bad answer is still bad. It is just bad with excellent latency. The handoff also matters. When should AI continue? When should a human step in? How should customers understand who they are talking to? What happens when the conversation moves from routine information to frustration, ambiguity, or money? These are design questions, not just technology questions. Companies often want AI chat because it reduces cost. Customers want AI chat only if it reduces effort. Those are not the same goal. When the system is designed around cost alone, customers feel trapped. When it is designed around resolution, AI can become genuinely useful. My takeaway: AI chat should be measured by whether it helps customers move forward, not whether it successfully keeps them away from humans. The best service automation knows when to answer, when to ask, and when to gracefully get out of the way.

title: ChatGPT made professional writing faster — and slightly more equal
excerpt: A story-first look at what happens when professionals use ChatGPT for everyday writing work: faster drafts, better output, and a surprising reduction in performance gaps.
content: Source: Noy & Zhang (2023) — “Experimental Evidence on the Productivity Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence,” Science I like papers that test AI on work that feels painfully normal. Not chess. Not benchmark puzzles. Not “can the model solve a problem invented by someone with too much coffee?” Just writing. Reports, emails, analysis plans, press releases. The sort of work that quietly eats the calendar and then pretends it was only a small task. This experiment gave 453 college-educated professionals realistic writing tasks and randomly gave half of them access to ChatGPT. The results were not subtle. Time fell by about 40%. Output quality rose by about 18%. That is already a big deal. But the part I find more interesting is the inequality result. ChatGPT helped lower-performing workers more, which narrowed the gap between stronger and weaker writers. In other words, AI did not just make everyone faster. It acted a little like a writing exoskeleton for people who needed more support. That has a very practical implication for organisations. If a task depends heavily on turning messy thoughts into acceptable prose, AI can raise the floor. The first draft becomes less terrifying. The blank page becomes less blank. People who might have spent twenty minutes politely wrestling with one paragraph can get to something usable much faster. Of course, this does not mean ChatGPT makes everyone brilliant. It means the boring middle layer of writing becomes cheaper. And that changes what we should value. If everyone can produce a decent draft faster, the advantage shifts toward knowing what to say, what not to say, and whether the draft is actually true. My takeaway: AI productivity is not just about speed. It changes where the human bottleneck sits. The writing gets easier. The judgment becomes more visible. Slightly inconvenient, but probably healthy.

title: In creative work, AI helps most when it critiques instead of performs
excerpt: A story-first look at why the same LLM can help or hurt creative work depending on whether it acts like a ghostwriter or a sounding board.
content: Source: Chen & Chan (2024) — “Large Language Model in Creative Work: The Role of Collaboration Modality and User Expertise,” Management Science There is a big difference between asking AI to think with you and asking AI to think instead of you. This paper made that difference very hard to ignore. The study looks at creative advertising work and separates two ways of using an LLM. In one mode, the AI acts like a ghostwriter: it generates the content and the human edits it. In the other, the AI acts like a sounding board: the human writes first, then the AI critiques. Same tool. Same general task. Very different outcomes. The finding I keep coming back to is that expertise changes the value of AI. For non-experts, AI critique can improve quality because it points out weaknesses they might not see. That feels intuitive. If you are learning, a good second opinion helps you notice what your eye has not yet learned to catch. But for experts, letting AI write the first draft can be dangerous. Not because experts become less capable overnight. Because the first draft quietly anchors the work. Once AI sets the shape, the human may spend more energy polishing than thinking. This is extremely relatable. Anyone who has edited a bad first draft knows the trap. At some point you are no longer asking, “Is this the right idea?” You are asking, “Can I make this sentence less embarrassing?” Different problem entirely 😭 The practical lesson is not “use AI” or “do not use AI.” It is: choose the collaboration mode carefully. If you need help seeing blind spots, use AI as a critic. If you need originality, judgment, or taste, be careful about handing over the first move. My takeaway: AI can make creative work better, but only if it stays in the right seat. Sometimes the best role for AI is not writer. It is the annoying but useful person asking, “Are you sure this is actually good?”

title: The future of work is not automation or augmentation — it is knowing which task gets which
excerpt: A story-first look at why AI should automate some tasks, assist humans on others, and leave the hardest work to people who still know what they are doing.
content: Source: Fügener, Walzner & Gupta (2026) — “Roles of Artificial Intelligence in Collaboration with Humans: Automation, Augmentation, and the Future of Work,” Management Science The AI-at-work debate often gets trapped in a very boring argument. Will AI replace people? Will AI assist people? Will AI create a magical workplace where everyone is productive and nobody has meetings that could have been emails? This paper is useful because it refuses the simple answer. It says the real question is task allocation. Some tasks should be automated. Some should be augmented. Some should stay with humans. That sounds obvious, but organisations are very talented at making obvious things complicated. The authors distinguish between two kinds of complementarity. Between-task complementarity means AI is better at some tasks and humans are better at others. In that case, automation makes sense because AI can take the easier or more AI-friendly work, freeing humans for harder tasks. Within-task complementarity means humans and AI perform better together on the same task. In that case, augmentation makes sense. The paper validates this with image-classification data. The pattern is elegant: AI automates relatively easy tasks, AI assists humans on tasks where their performance is similar, and humans work alone on the hardest tasks. I like this because it sounds much more realistic than “AI everywhere.” Not every task needs a human-AI collaboration layer. Sometimes AI should just do the thing. Sometimes the human needs advice. Sometimes the human needs quiet, context, and freedom from another dashboard pretending to help. The hidden lesson is resource reallocation. Automation only creates value if the humans freed from routine work are moved to work where they actually add value. Otherwise, AI just creates spare capacity that disappears into more meetings. Tragic but believable. My takeaway: the future of work is not about choosing automation or augmentation as a slogan. It is about knowing where each one belongs. The hard part is not the model. It is the job design.

title: Social bots can make people engage — but not always in the way platforms hope
excerpt: A story-first look at social bots on microblogging platforms: they can increase engagement, but may also train users to post for the bot instead of for each other.
content: Source: Gao, Zhang & Lysyakov (2025) — “Does Social Bot Help Socialize? Evidence from a Microblogging Platform,” Information Systems Research There is something slightly funny about platforms using bots to make humans more social. It feels like hosting a dinner party and hiring a robot to laugh at everyone’s jokes so the guests feel encouraged. This paper studies exactly that kind of situation. A microblogging platform launched a platform-owned social bot called CommentRobot. The bot generated comments under posts, and the researchers studied whether that public bot interaction increased user engagement. The short answer is yes. Posts that received bot-generated comments saw more engagement. An online experiment confirmed the effect and showed that both bot identity and comment quality mattered. Good bot comments were attractive, relevant, and included social cues. In other words, people responded not just because something commented, but because the comment felt socially useful. That is the encouraging part. The awkward part is what happened next. Receiving bot comments encouraged users to create more bot-related posts, but it did not necessarily increase overall posting activity. So the bot helped socialize at the post level, but it did not magically revive the whole platform. This is where the finding becomes very practical. AI can stimulate engagement, but engagement is not always the same as community. A bot comment can make a post feel less lonely. It can create a nudge, a cue, a little spark. But if users begin posting for the bot instead of for other people, the platform may get activity without the deeper social value it wanted. That feels like a very 2026 problem: the metric improves, but the meaning is questionable. My takeaway: social bots can help, but deployment strategy matters. The goal should not be “make the numbers move.” It should be to create interactions humans still find worth joining. Otherwise, everyone is just performing for the machine, which is a bit too on the nose.

title: ChatGPT is becoming a shopping channel, but not yet a shopping monster
excerpt: A story-first look at ChatGPT referrals to e-commerce sites: LLM traffic is real, growing, and useful for complex products, but it is still a niche channel.
content: Source: Kaiser & Schulze (2026) — “Frontiers: ChatGPT Referrals to E-Commerce Websites,” Marketing Science At some point, shopping quietly moved from search boxes to conversations. Instead of typing “best espresso machine under $500” into Google and opening fourteen tabs like a person pretending to be organised, people can now ask ChatGPT and get comparisons, explanations, and purchase links. This paper asks a very practical question: is ChatGPT referral traffic actually valuable for e-commerce? The authors study 12 months of first-party data from 973 websites, covering more than 50,000 ChatGPT-referred transactions and 164 million transactions from traditional channels. So this is not a small “my cousin clicked a link once” dataset. It is serious. The result is balanced. Organic LLM traffic converts better than paid social, but worse than most traditional channels. Revenue per session is modest. Volume is still low. Engagement looks mixed: bounce rates are favourable, but session duration and page views are lower. The interesting twist is product complexity. ChatGPT referrals perform better for complex product categories. That makes sense. If I am buying socks, I do not need a conversation. If I am buying an espresso machine, insurance product, camera, or anything with too many tabs and opinions, I suddenly appreciate an assistant who can explain trade-offs without judging me. So ChatGPT is not replacing search overnight. But it is becoming a new kind of channel: less like advertising, more like assisted decision-making. That matters because marketing teams love declaring channels either dead or revolutionary. This one is neither. At least not yet. My takeaway: LLM referrals are real, but early. They currently serve niche informational needs, especially for complex purchases. The bigger shift is not traffic volume today. It is that consumers may increasingly start shopping by asking questions instead of searching keywords. That changes the game quietly first, then suddenly.

title: The best human-algorithm teams know when to disagree
excerpt: A story-first look at loan evaluation experiments showing that human-algorithm collaboration works best when humans disagree with algorithms at the right time.
content: Source: Wang, Zhang & Lu (2025) — “The Power of Disagreement: A Field Experiment to Investigate Human-Algorithm Collaboration in Loan Evaluations,” Management Science Human-algorithm collaboration sounds lovely until the human and the algorithm disagree. Then suddenly everyone becomes very philosophical. Do we trust the model? Do we trust the human? Do we ask for another dashboard? Do we form a committee and lose the will to live? This paper studies disagreement in loan evaluations, which is exactly the kind of setting where the stakes are high and the phrase “just follow the algorithm” feels a little too casual. The researchers ran a field experiment where human evaluators and algorithms worked together to assess loan applications. The key question was not whether humans should always follow or always override the model. It was whether humans could disagree at the right time. That phrase matters. Bad disagreement is just ego with a spreadsheet. The human ignores the algorithm because they “have a feeling.” Very cinematic, not always useful. Good disagreement happens when the algorithm is wrong and the human catches it. The study finds that human-algorithm collaboration can outperform either humans or algorithms alone, but the value depends on how disagreement forms and whether it is effective. One especially interesting finding is that algorithm self-contradiction can trigger useful disagreement. When the model’s rationale or signals do not fully line up, humans become more alert and are better able to challenge the recommendation at the right moment. I love this because it reframes disagreement as a feature, not a failure. The goal of human-in-the-loop systems is not blind agreement. If the human always agrees with the algorithm, why is the human there? Decoration? My takeaway: collaboration value comes from structured friction. The best systems do not just tell humans what the algorithm thinks. They help humans notice when the algorithm may be wrong. That is where judgment earns its seat.

title: The quantum threat is not a future problem — it's already happening
excerpt: This is one of those risks that sounds abstract until you imagine explaining it after the fact. Then it suddenly becomes very concrete, very expensive, and very difficult...
content: Source: Google Security Blog — “The Quantum Era Is Coming. Are We Ready to Secure It?” This is one of those risks that sounds abstract until you imagine explaining it after the fact. Then it suddenly becomes very concrete, very expensive, and very difficult to hide behind a slide deck. I used to think quantum security was one of those future problems. You know, the kind of thing people discuss in conference panels with very serious faces, then everyone goes back to worrying about passwords, phishing emails, and why someone still has access to a system they left three jobs ago. But this Google Security Blog post made me pause. The scary part is not that quantum computers can already break modern encryption at scale. The scary part is that attackers do not need to wait. They can steal encrypted data today and store it for later. Then, when quantum computers become powerful enough, they come back and decrypt it. This has a very calm name: “store now, decrypt later.” Personally, I think the name is too polite. It sounds like a cloud storage feature. It is actually more like someone quietly photocopying your locked diary because they know they will find the key in a few years 😭 That is what makes this risk so strange. Most security problems feel immediate. Someone has to explain the incident to management while pretending they slept. The damage may happen later, but the exposure starts now. In plain English, that is why the result matters beyond the chart. It changes where people should look, what they should question, and which comfortable assumption probably needs to be retired. My takeaway: the danger is rarely the dramatic thing in the headline. It is the quiet gap between knowing a risk exists and assigning someone to do something about it. Very unglamorous. Very important.

title: The AI Cost-Cutting Dilemma
excerpt: This is one of those studies where the headline is only the doorway. The useful part is what happens after you walk through it and realise the practical question is...
content: This is one of those studies where the headline is only the doorway. The useful part is what happens after you walk through it and realise the practical question is messier than expected. Software is expensive, but running software is often even more expensive. One estimate I keep seeing is that for every $1 spent on software, companies may spend around $6 on services, implementation, support, and operations. So the promise of AI agents is very tempting: less manual work, fewer handovers, faster execution, lower cost. But here is the dilemma I keep thinking about. AI is getting very good at “junior work”. For many companies, the question becomes: if an AI agent can do this faster and cheaper, why hire the junior person? But then, where do seniors come from? People become good by doing the boring first drafts, making mistakes, sitting in meetings they barely understand, watching how senior people think, getting corrected, and trying again. If we remove too much of the junior layer, we may save cost today but damage the talent pipeline tomorrow. This matters especially in Asia, where entry-level jobs are often the first bridge into the professional economy. So maybe the question is not whether AI should replace juniors. The better question is: How do we redesign junior roles so people learn with AI, not disappear because of AI? Because a company with no juniors today may become an industry with no experts tomorrow. In plain English, that is why the result matters beyond the chart. It changes where people should look, what they should question, and which comfortable assumption probably needs to be retired. That is the version of AI progress I find most believable. Not magic. Not doom. Just new leverage, new failure modes, and a slightly larger responsibility bill.

title: Ghostwriter or sounding board — the collaboration mode matters more than the AI itself
excerpt: The thing I like about this paper is that it complicates the easy story. It is not simply “AI good” or “AI bad.” It is more like: AI changes the work, and then the real...
content: Source: Chen & Chan (2024) — “Large Language Model in Creative Work: The Role of Collaboration Modality and User Expertise,” Management Science The thing I like about this paper is that it complicates the easy story. It is not simply “AI good” or “AI bad.” It is more like: AI changes the work, and then the real problem moves somewhere less obvious. Here’s a finding I keep thinking about: two groups of people use the same AI tool for the same creative task. One group sees their output quality go up. The difference isn’t the AI — it’s how they used it. This paper runs a controlled experiment where expert and non-expert users write advertising copy with and without LLM assistance.
